doc.title: Chuck Mancuso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 10, 2013

title: Becoming a jazz fan through his father's 78s
summary: Monk Rowe introduces Mancuso; he recalls boogie woogie records at age nine or ten, his father's Frankie Carle taste, and reading everything on music with no one to share it.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: My name is Monk Rowe and I am in the office in Buffalo of Chuck Mancuso. And I’m glad to be here at Buffalo State College. And I’m going to describe you as, well first of all, a professor of music, but researcher and author, and a huge fan — is that where it started, as being a huge fan — of this music?

Yeah, right. It started back in the 50s, and I was just a kid playing a lot of sports and I thought I was going to be a sports writer. And I found out that this great music that I loved — you know my father had these 78s, and when we were little kids both mom and dad worked, and so they’d say on Saturday mornings you’ve got to be quiet, because we’re upstairs sleeping in the house. So I went through his records. I mean I was what, maybe nine, ten years old. And the first things that hit me were those boogie woogie things of Pete Johnson. I’d go oh my God, this is so cool, and then Albert Ammons and the rest of them. He was a big Frankie Carle fan.

Right. He was very florid and fluid and you know, romantic. And my father was — he wasn’t a musician, my mother wasn’t a musician. No one had any instruments in the house. But I got stung. And as the years went on I started reading every book I could. And one summer I’d just read Hemingway, Storm Jamesen and a number of others that had nothing to do with music. And another summer it was all the beat generation. But other summers it was just music. Just all the things I could get on jazz and pop and everything else. And I always wondered why they never taught this stuff in school because it was so fascinating, and I had no one to talk to, there was no one to share it with.
I was going to say, you couldn’t have had many friends that were boys that were your age that would like go, “So what do you think of James P. Johnson?”
